Statistics is the&nbsp; art of lying by means of figures. That quote&nbsp;&nbsp; really stuck with me. As it turns out, if you're&nbsp; clever, you can use data to prove almost any point&nbsp;&nbsp; you want. or worse, data can convince you of a&nbsp; false truth. Data can be very useful in convincing&nbsp;&nbsp; your development teammates of a design direction,&nbsp; but it's much less useful for finding the right&nbsp;&nbsp; tuning decision to make for your audience.&nbsp; Checking telemetry from League of Legends,&nbsp;&nbsp; you might find that the item Maji Soulstealer has&nbsp; an absurdly high win rate, often close to 80%. But&nbsp;&nbsp; this statistic is highly misleading. The item is&nbsp; rarely purchased unless you're already winning,&nbsp;&nbsp; which means the player purchasing it was already&nbsp; very likely to win before making the purchase. The&nbsp;&nbsp; developers understood why the win rate for this&nbsp; item was the way it was, and that kept them from&nbsp;&nbsp; making the mistake of trusting the numbers alone&nbsp; and making a poor tuning decision. This means that&nbsp;&nbsp; in order to find guidance within the numbers, you&nbsp; need an extraordinary amount of context. Let's say&nbsp;&nbsp; that you look at your character pick rates and&nbsp; one of the characters is very underreresented.&nbsp;&nbsp; Do we have any idea why just from the numbers&nbsp; alone? Is it because the characters too weak?&nbsp;&nbsp; Or are they difficult to use? Or do they lose&nbsp; matchups to some of the most common characters?&nbsp;&nbsp; Or are they just kind of ugly? Without the&nbsp; reason why, this data is effectively useless&nbsp;&nbsp; as a means to understanding what changes to make&nbsp; in your game. Early on in Overwatch's lifespan,&nbsp;&nbsp; developers saw the use rate of the support hero&nbsp; Symmetra was low. And so on December 13th, 2016,&nbsp;&nbsp; they overhauled the character, changing the way&nbsp; her move set worked. Developer design notes said&nbsp;&nbsp; they wanted to make Symmetra feel more active&nbsp; and give her more meaningful contributions to the&nbsp;&nbsp; team. Overall, Symmetra players liked the changes,&nbsp; but the use rate barely went up. The players were&nbsp;&nbsp; somewhat happy, but the goal of normalizing the&nbsp; use rate was not achieved. She still wasn't very&nbsp;&nbsp; popular. On June 26th, 2018, a year and a half&nbsp; later, Symmetra was reworked a second time. This&nbsp;&nbsp; time, moving her from a support role into a damage&nbsp; role. Many Symmetra players lost their fun in this&nbsp;&nbsp; overhaul, and some physically disabled players&nbsp; could no longer play the character at all. The&nbsp;&nbsp; use rate dropped below the original version&nbsp; while simultaneously making the player base&nbsp;&nbsp; upset without understanding why the use rate&nbsp; was low to begin with, tuning the character,&nbsp;&nbsp; or worse, reworking them entirely is like throwing&nbsp; darts while blindfolded after being punched in the&nbsp;&nbsp; face. Was the pick rate low because Symmetra was&nbsp; weak? Or was it because her toolkit didn't fit in&nbsp;&nbsp; well with the dominant strategies running the&nbsp; game? Or was it because she was only fun to a&nbsp;&nbsp; certain type of player? And if I may ask, is&nbsp; it even a problem that her pick rate was low&nbsp;&nbsp; or that the game has niche characters that aren't&nbsp; tournament viable? Well, is it? Without context,&nbsp;&nbsp; data is often worse than useless. It can make you&nbsp; think a problem exists where there isn't one, and&nbsp;&nbsp; it might lead you to making decisions that remove&nbsp; the fun of some of your players. Data without&nbsp;&nbsp; context is dangerous. We should also consider that&nbsp; data is almost never qualitative and it's easily&nbsp;&nbsp; skewed. Developers that use telemetry to observe&nbsp; the win rates of various characters and weapons&nbsp;&nbsp; will find obvious and large differences when they&nbsp; start to sort that data by player rank. But can&nbsp;&nbsp; we really trust a qualifier like player rank to&nbsp; sort and understand this data? Ranking systems&nbsp;&nbsp; are only good at sorting people who use them a&nbsp; lot. Consider that there are tournament level&nbsp;&nbsp; players who do not play ranked mode often at all.&nbsp; and when they do, they may be much lower ranked&nbsp;&nbsp; than their actual skill level due to their lack of&nbsp; ranked play time. You must also realize that not&nbsp;&nbsp; everyone in the top ranking bracket is of equal&nbsp; skill. And so this can affect a character's win&nbsp;&nbsp; rate rather drastically, even within that segment&nbsp; of players. And within that segment, you may find&nbsp;&nbsp; that certain strategies or characters are barely&nbsp; used at all. Think about what else goes into the&nbsp;&nbsp; win rate. This a 1v one game or a team game. Is&nbsp; the character difficult or easy to use? How do&nbsp;&nbsp; we interpret the stats of a character who thrives&nbsp; in online matchmaking but struggles to place well&nbsp;&nbsp; in full tournament brackets? How close are the&nbsp; game's best character specialists to reaching&nbsp;&nbsp; each character's known potential? And what don't&nbsp; we know about a character's potential? Even if we&nbsp;&nbsp; could perfectly understand the quality of our win&nbsp; rate data, we simply can't learn enough from it to&nbsp;&nbsp; identify if we even have a problem to address,&nbsp; let alone possible solutions to that problem.&nbsp;&nbsp; Maybe we can spot a lopsided matchup with data&nbsp; from time to time, which can be really helpful&nbsp;&nbsp; in knowing where to look, but it isn't at all&nbsp; helpful in figuring out what to change. Remember,&nbsp;&nbsp; data will lie to you. Using Street Fighter 6's&nbsp; publicly available telemetry, we can see such&nbsp;&nbsp; a case in action. Doulam, Lily, Honda, Rasheed,&nbsp; Blanca, and Kimberly are the bottom six characters&nbsp;&nbsp; in terms of use rates and ranked, both across all&nbsp; ranks overall and when isolating the master ranked&nbsp;&nbsp; players. And yet the characters with the highest&nbsp; win rates in master rank are in order Ponda,&nbsp;&nbsp; Kimberly, Dawson, JP, Blanca, Rasheed. So this is&nbsp; almost the exact inverse. And player conceptions&nbsp;&nbsp; of these characters place in the tier lists bear&nbsp; no relation to any of this data. Most players&nbsp;&nbsp; think Blanca and Rasheed are high tier. Honda&nbsp; and Lily are low tier. And ideas about Doulam&nbsp;&nbsp; and Kimberly's strength vary wildly. This data&nbsp; could easily lead you to believe that these six&nbsp;&nbsp; characters are weak due to underuse or make you&nbsp; think that they're too strong because of their&nbsp;&nbsp; high win rates. Data without context is dangerous.&nbsp; Yes, but even trying to apply proper context to&nbsp;&nbsp; your data is almost impossibly difficult. So,&nbsp; if we can't really trust data to guide us,&nbsp;&nbsp; we should probably talk to the players in our&nbsp; community, right? After all, they play the most.&nbsp;&nbsp; They're often extremely skilled and they know the&nbsp; game pretty pretty damn well. Well, unfortunately,&nbsp;&nbsp; even though most of them don't mean to, players&nbsp; frequently lie, too. If you've been in or around&nbsp;&nbsp; gamedev long enough, you've certainly heard the&nbsp; phrase, "Players don't know what they want." This&nbsp;&nbsp; isn't entirely true in my experience. There's&nbsp; a relatively well-known clip of me from the&nbsp;&nbsp; wonderful fight on Killer Instinct documentary by&nbsp; Hold Back to Block, in which I tell an anecdote&nbsp;&nbsp; about a time when the KI community rallied&nbsp; together and really wanted us to nerf JGO.&nbsp;&nbsp; Specifically, his ability to heal himself by&nbsp; landing fireballs during his instinct mode&nbsp;&nbsp; made them feel like they had to kill him three&nbsp; times instead of two. But nerfing his healing,&nbsp;&nbsp; as they had requested, would have cut away at the&nbsp; character's core identity and a large part of what&nbsp;&nbsp; makes him unique and fun to play. The community&nbsp; was laser focused on seeing the healing as the&nbsp;&nbsp; problem. And their view of the game was that&nbsp; JGO was either too strong or too frustrating to&nbsp;&nbsp; play against depending on who you asked. Whether&nbsp; this was the true state of the game or not is not&nbsp;&nbsp; relevant. They believed JGO was a problem and&nbsp; their perception, no matter how flawed, is the&nbsp;&nbsp; reality they live in. To tune games properly, you&nbsp; must accept this. A player's perception is their&nbsp;&nbsp; reality. So instead of succumbing to the community&nbsp; pressure campaign and nerfing Jgo's healing,&nbsp;&nbsp; we took a different approach that allowed us to&nbsp; maintain his fun and unique healing gimmick while&nbsp;&nbsp; weakening some of the more brainless parts of&nbsp; his kit that allowed him to negate his intended&nbsp;&nbsp; weaknesses too easily. The community cooked us&nbsp; pretty hard for a few weeks, insisting that this&nbsp;&nbsp; wasn't the change they asked for and wouldn't&nbsp; make a difference. But a few weeks after that,&nbsp;&nbsp; complaining about JGO had all but stopped.&nbsp; Players knew they wanted a weaker JGO. It's just&nbsp;&nbsp; that their idea of how to do it would have had way&nbsp; worse knockdown effects on the game and JGO player&nbsp;&nbsp; base than what we landed on. And of course, a very&nbsp; small number of JGO players were unable to adapt&nbsp;&nbsp; to the changes that we did end up going with, and&nbsp; they either switched characters or quit the game&nbsp;&nbsp; entirely. That sucks, but it's a natural part of&nbsp; the tuning process. You can't please everyone,&nbsp;&nbsp; but you can limit the negative blowback of a nerf&nbsp; if you're thoughtful. Was Jgo too strong on paper?&nbsp;&nbsp; Did he even need to be nerfed in the first place?&nbsp; Believe it or not, it doesn't actually matter.&nbsp;&nbsp; Ultimately, players were frustrated and something&nbsp; had to be done about that. The something we chose&nbsp;&nbsp; weakened JGO, which is what the players wanted,&nbsp; but the way we did it strayed pretty far from most&nbsp;&nbsp; of the common complaints. So, in a way, players&nbsp; do occasionally know what they want. It's just&nbsp;&nbsp; that they don't usually know the least destructive&nbsp; way to get there. Most of your user base will lie&nbsp;&nbsp; to you, but I'll state again, they usually don't&nbsp; mean to. They're generally well-intentioned, and&nbsp;&nbsp; they just want the game to get better. But better&nbsp; for who? Even among the most well-meaning users,&nbsp;&nbsp; you'll find that the overwhelming majority&nbsp; of them struggle to see the big picture or&nbsp;&nbsp; consider the viewpoints of others. Their idea of&nbsp; a better game is very commonly one in which they&nbsp;&nbsp; with their character or weapon of choice can win&nbsp; more easily. Things that beat their play style get&nbsp;&nbsp; weakened and their play style gets stronger and no&nbsp; one complains about their play style so they can&nbsp;&nbsp; feel good about using it. I used to think this way&nbsp; myself, so I'm not trying to cut you down if you&nbsp;&nbsp; currently think this way. It goes without saying&nbsp; that this isn't a good way to make a more fair or&nbsp;&nbsp; less frustrating game. So, you need to take every&nbsp; piece of feedback that you get with a massive&nbsp;&nbsp; grain of salt and try to apply as much context to&nbsp; it as possible. Developers can be easily misled&nbsp;&nbsp; by data, sure, but they can even more easily&nbsp; be misled by players. Data can be convincing,&nbsp;&nbsp; but players can be very, very loud and hard to&nbsp; ignore. It is, of course, not possible to know&nbsp;&nbsp; what you don't currently know. But that won't stop&nbsp; players from insisting that their perspective is&nbsp;&nbsp; the truth. After all, to them, it currently is.&nbsp; But their perspective can shift quickly. Players&nbsp;&nbsp; are very easily influenced and misled. Influencer&nbsp; types can often without even meaning to construct&nbsp;&nbsp; completely false narratives that large swaths&nbsp; of your user base will bandwagon on and help&nbsp;&nbsp; amplify. Suddenly, the desires or misinformation&nbsp; of just one popular player can start to sound&nbsp;&nbsp; like hundreds or thousands of people who all agree&nbsp; about what the problem is and how to fix it. Group&nbsp;&nbsp; think is a major issue that puts a lot of social&nbsp; pressure on devs that can be very difficult to&nbsp;&nbsp; navigate. And it isn't just influential players or&nbsp; malicious players who can influence a crowd. It's&nbsp;&nbsp; often tournament results themselves. Early on,&nbsp; after the launch of Injustice 2 in May of 2017,&nbsp;&nbsp; generational talent, Sonic Fox, won nearly every&nbsp; tournament they attended using Captain Cold, a&nbsp;&nbsp; character that many at the time thought was on the&nbsp; weaker end of the roster. Sonic Fox's dominant win&nbsp;&nbsp; streak resulted in a community that was forced to&nbsp; reassess the actual strength of the character. and&nbsp;&nbsp; eventually developers that nerfed the character&nbsp; despite Sonic Fox's insistence that Captain Cold&nbsp;&nbsp; was indeed weak and just counterpicked certain&nbsp; characters well. But you don't even have to go&nbsp;&nbsp; on a dominant winning streak to change people's&nbsp; views. After Super Street Fighter 4 launched in&nbsp;&nbsp; April of 2010, right before tournament season&nbsp; really kicked off, many of us looked to our&nbsp;&nbsp; strongest players to assess the power levels&nbsp; of the 10 new characters that were added to&nbsp;&nbsp; the roster. Going into EVO 2010 on July 9th,&nbsp; the widespread sentiment among top players was&nbsp;&nbsp; that Adon was among the weaker characters added&nbsp; to the game. Many of us went into that event,&nbsp;&nbsp; writing the character off completely. And then&nbsp; gamer B took fifth place out of about 1,700&nbsp;&nbsp; players with ADON that weekend in the largest&nbsp; open bracket tournament we had seen to date.&nbsp;&nbsp; Totally upending how we viewed the character&nbsp; for months without a single balance change. Gamer B from Taiwan using Adom. For all you people&nbsp; out there, don't believe that Adon can take it to&nbsp;&nbsp; the top eight. In an even more dramatic example,&nbsp; let's look at Super Smash Brothers Melee. One of&nbsp;&nbsp; the most popular competitive games of all time&nbsp; and a game that has not been patched since the&nbsp;&nbsp; 1.02 Players Choice discs were released in 2003.&nbsp; Melee has a very long and welldocumented history&nbsp;&nbsp; of community agreed upon tier lists to rank&nbsp; the strongest and weakest characters. By all&nbsp;&nbsp; conventional wisdom, Yoshi sat as the 21st best&nbsp; character in the game in a roster of 26. Not good.&nbsp;&nbsp; And then AMSA appeared in the tournament scene&nbsp; and started getting results with Yoshi. Yoshi's&nbsp;&nbsp; rank went from 21st to 12th from 2013 to 2015.&nbsp; And after AMSA's win at Big House 10 in October&nbsp;&nbsp; of 2022, arguably the hardest melee major of all&nbsp; time, Yoshi now sits as the 10th best character&nbsp;&nbsp; in the game on community tier lists. Despite&nbsp; nothing about the game changing, Yoshi rose 11&nbsp;&nbsp; spots in the ranks. Yoshi is the best of the 987&nbsp; competitors. Again, we simply cannot know what we&nbsp;&nbsp; do not know. Whether it's Sonic Fox thinking&nbsp; their tournament winning character is weak,&nbsp;&nbsp; or a consensus of top players thinking that&nbsp; a character they don't even man is weak just&nbsp;&nbsp; before a breakout performance, or AMSA believing&nbsp; in their characters power despite ridiculous&nbsp;&nbsp; execution requirements and being the only one&nbsp; in the world who can do it. It just goes to show&nbsp;&nbsp; you how easily players and developer opinions can&nbsp; be swayed by tournament results and influencers.&nbsp;&nbsp; When group think and player pressure campaigns&nbsp; arrive at your doorstep, it's incredibly hard,&nbsp;&nbsp; maybe impossible as a developer to know what&nbsp; situation you're actually in and guess right. Is&nbsp;&nbsp; the character weak or strong? Without many years&nbsp; of evidence, you'll have to make an assumption.&nbsp;&nbsp; You'll be right sometimes, and you'll be wrong&nbsp; other times, and it's a huge part of why tuning&nbsp;&nbsp; a competitive game is so difficult. And of course,&nbsp; when talking about our inability to know what we&nbsp;&nbsp; don't yet know and how that influences the way we&nbsp; think about our passions in the world, I need to&nbsp;&nbsp; remind you, dear viewer, of the Dunning Krueger&nbsp; effect. We can be extremely confident that we&nbsp;&nbsp; know everything about the state of a game when we,&nbsp; in fact, are only seeing a small part of the big&nbsp;&nbsp; picture. Even the strongest players in the world&nbsp; who are regularly winning tournaments may only be&nbsp;&nbsp; aware of a tiny fraction of what's possible within&nbsp; a play space. And while balanced discussions and&nbsp;&nbsp; tierless theorizing can be incredibly fun, it is&nbsp; for these reasons that players make misleading and&nbsp;&nbsp; unreliable sources of guidance when deciding how&nbsp; to tune your game. Okay, so we can't rely on data&nbsp;&nbsp; or players for guidance. But what about the goals&nbsp; we'd set out to achieve in the first place? Let's&nbsp;&nbsp; examine our list of goals and try to understand&nbsp; if we're even attempting to steer in the right&nbsp;&nbsp; direction. Goal number one, a favorite goal of&nbsp; players is fairness. Fairness should not and&nbsp;&nbsp; cannot ever be a goal. Why? Because no two players&nbsp; can ever universally agree on what is fair. It's&nbsp;&nbsp; an emotional metric that changes by the minute&nbsp; depending on who you ask, the results of their&nbsp;&nbsp; latest ranked match, what salty player showed up&nbsp; on their social media algorithm that day. It is&nbsp;&nbsp; simply not an achievable goal because game balance&nbsp; is mostly vibes. You cannot measure your success&nbsp;&nbsp; by measuring fairness as the only way to do so.&nbsp; Data or player surveys are frequently misleading.&nbsp;&nbsp; Remember, as a developer, you also don't know what&nbsp; you don't know. Things you think you know may be&nbsp;&nbsp; false, and you are just as easy to manipulate&nbsp; as the players are. Remember that League of&nbsp;&nbsp; Legends example from the start of the video about&nbsp; Vladimir Sanguin Pool? That wasn't the only time&nbsp;&nbsp; something like that happened in League. When the&nbsp; champion Riven was released, she was viewed by the&nbsp;&nbsp; community as weak. Riot devs apparently agreed and&nbsp; hotfixed in some buffs for the character. Shortly&nbsp;&nbsp; after posting the hot fix notes on the forums, the&nbsp; character's play rate spiked and the feedback was&nbsp;&nbsp; very positive. Players reported how good the buffs&nbsp; felt and what a difference they made, but the hot&nbsp;&nbsp; fix hadn't actually gone live yet. The character&nbsp; was unchanged. Game balance is mostly vibes. The&nbsp;&nbsp; idea of fairness is so individual to each player&nbsp; that it can never be an achievable or even&nbsp;&nbsp; measurable goal. Even when group think makes it&nbsp; seem like thousands of players have the same view&nbsp;&nbsp; on an issue, their overall feelings of fairness&nbsp; will differ greatly. Only way to tune your game&nbsp;&nbsp; into a state in which no player is complaining is&nbsp; to make them all quit. Because of these reasons,&nbsp;&nbsp; I strongly recommend that we stop using the idea&nbsp; of fairness as a tuning goal. Goal number two,&nbsp;&nbsp; a favorite goal of viewers is variety. But&nbsp; variety is not the result of mathematical&nbsp;&nbsp; balance or fairness. It's the result of enabling&nbsp; diverse player expression. Let me explain why.&nbsp;&nbsp; Each individual player has their own play style&nbsp; and their own view on what aspects of your game&nbsp;&nbsp; or characters are fun. This includes the type of&nbsp; risks different players want to take when trying&nbsp;&nbsp; to win. Some players want to play it as safe as&nbsp; possible and focus on reactions with a low-risk,&nbsp;&nbsp; lowreward strategy. Other players may want&nbsp; to gamble, taking big bets and trying to get&nbsp;&nbsp; maximum rewards. And everything in between those&nbsp; two extremes exists as well. If a character is&nbsp;&nbsp; harder to learn and pilot and optimize, should&nbsp; that character be equal in theoretical power&nbsp;&nbsp; output with a character that's trivial to learn&nbsp; and pilot and optimize? An easy character could be&nbsp;&nbsp; considered low risk. A difficult character could&nbsp; be considered high risk. If both risks result in&nbsp;&nbsp; the same reward, which character will most players&nbsp; choose? Or to put it more plainly, one character's&nbsp;&nbsp; low risk, high reward, and the other one is high&nbsp; risk, high reward? What I've observed over the&nbsp;&nbsp; years is that when a game is tuned toward a more&nbsp; flat mathematical balance, play styles start to&nbsp;&nbsp; converge. When this happens, players gravitate&nbsp; towards one of two types of characters. They'll&nbsp;&nbsp; either play the characters that are easiest to win&nbsp; with, thus lowering their risk, or they'll play&nbsp;&nbsp; the characters that look the coolest or sexiest&nbsp; because the vibes matter a lot to us. And watch&nbsp;&nbsp; out if your easy characters are also your coolest&nbsp; ones. We won't often achieve tournament variety by&nbsp;&nbsp; flattening win rate and use rates because doing&nbsp; so flattens out the number of reasons different&nbsp;&nbsp; players gravitate toward different characters&nbsp; or play patterns. It's the quantity of different&nbsp;&nbsp; motivators that you offer to your players&nbsp; that breeds variety. Despite not being widely&nbsp;&nbsp; considered to have the most balanced roster, the&nbsp; original version of Guilty Gear Xer sign would&nbsp;&nbsp; frequently see large variety of characters in&nbsp; tournament top eights. Why? because the characters&nbsp;&nbsp; are so different and diverse that they appeal&nbsp; strongly to different player types. Conversely,&nbsp;&nbsp; in the Tekken series, many of the characters share&nbsp; variations of the same game plan and have similar&nbsp;&nbsp; riskreward values. But in Guilty Gear, almost&nbsp; no characters play even remotely alike. This&nbsp;&nbsp; is why when Tekken misses the mark, it's much more&nbsp; common to see something like four Bobs in a Tekken&nbsp;&nbsp; 6 top eight like at EVO 2011, or six Leroys in a&nbsp; Tekken 7 top eight like at EVO Japan in 2020. If&nbsp;&nbsp; the Guilty Gear developers worked hard to flatten&nbsp; the game using data, they'd end up destroying many&nbsp;&nbsp; players favorite play styles and the result would&nbsp; almost certainly be a game with less variety for&nbsp;&nbsp; viewers. And we did in fact end up seeing this&nbsp; in motion at the launch of Guilty Gear Strive,&nbsp;&nbsp; which had top eights dominated by many appearances&nbsp; of Soul Bad Guy, a character boasting the trifecta&nbsp;&nbsp; of easy to use, powerful, and super cool. Because&nbsp; at launch, Strive was more simple and many of the&nbsp;&nbsp; characters felt more sy than in past iterations&nbsp; of the franchise, players gravitated towards this&nbsp;&nbsp; very easy and powerful badass. Down the line, as&nbsp; new mechanics and extremely unique characters were&nbsp;&nbsp; added to the roster, tournament variety improved a&nbsp; great deal. As a goal, variety is an admirable and&nbsp;&nbsp; understandable one. It's actually measurable with&nbsp; telemetry or by looking at tournament results. And&nbsp;&nbsp; if you aren't hitting a good level of variety,&nbsp; your player base will absolutely let you know.&nbsp;&nbsp; But unfortunately, I believe that you'll have&nbsp; a much harder time achieving variety by making&nbsp;&nbsp; it your end goal. Variety is a symptom of a&nbsp; healthy game ecosystem, not the result of a&nbsp;&nbsp; mathematically balanced game. Variety has another&nbsp; enemy, optimization of play patterns, which I'm&nbsp;&nbsp; going to talk more about later. And finally, the&nbsp; third goal that we skipped over at the beginning,&nbsp;&nbsp; the only real and true goal worth pursuing with&nbsp; game tuning efforts, player retention. Retention&nbsp;&nbsp; is all about making your existing players want&nbsp; to play more or at a bare minimum preventing them&nbsp;&nbsp; from quitting. Fairness is a cute idea. Variety&nbsp; is nice to have if you can get it, but if players&nbsp;&nbsp; aren't playing, there isn't any point to anything&nbsp; you might change in your game. We tune the game&nbsp;&nbsp; and engage with players so that they'll continue&nbsp; playing. That is the goal. We already discussed&nbsp;&nbsp; why players quit and among the reasons within our&nbsp; control are that they get too frustrated or the&nbsp;&nbsp; gameplay stops being thoughtful and engaging. so&nbsp; they get bored. Using this, we can break down our&nbsp;&nbsp; main retention goal into smaller parts. We need&nbsp; to A reduce player frustration, b increase and&nbsp;&nbsp; reinforce thoughtful play patterns that result in&nbsp; engagement, and C do all of that while trying to&nbsp;&nbsp; enable and maintain a high level of diverse&nbsp; player expression. Easy, right? Naturally,&nbsp;&nbsp; doing all of those things while keeping a&nbsp; community happy with the direction you're going&nbsp;&nbsp; is not so easy after all. But in my experience,&nbsp; there are strategies you can use to make it work.&nbsp;&nbsp; So, here's my approach to game tuning with those&nbsp; goals in mind. To the developers watching this,&nbsp;&nbsp; the tuning strategies and methodologies I use&nbsp; work for me. They might work for you or they&nbsp;&nbsp; might not. My goal is to share with you what I've&nbsp; learned so that you can use the parts that make&nbsp;&nbsp; sense for you and your project. Just remember to&nbsp; always be critical about what you use and why.&nbsp;&nbsp; To players watching this, I hope you take away&nbsp; an improved vocabulary about game tuning and a&nbsp;&nbsp; wider view of what the goals of game tuning really&nbsp; are. And I hope that you can use this to improve&nbsp;&nbsp; the way you communicate with developers and each&nbsp; other. The classical approach of using data as&nbsp;&nbsp; a metric to measure the success of your tuning&nbsp; efforts is what I'll call tuning for flatness,&nbsp;&nbsp; wherein you try to achieve fairness and variety&nbsp; by normalizing telemetry and survey data. But&nbsp;&nbsp; when tuning, you need to approach the problem less&nbsp; like a banker balancing the books and more like a&nbsp;&nbsp; beekeeper making sure that the hive is healthy&nbsp; and thriving. Imagine that you're responsible&nbsp;&nbsp; for balancing the environment of Earth and you&nbsp; get a data report and discover that there are 20&nbsp;&nbsp; quadrillion ants on the planet but only 3 trillion&nbsp; trees. If you believe this is an imbalance, you&nbsp;&nbsp; aren't in the right mindset to tune a competitive&nbsp; game. A version of Earth with 20 quadrillion trees&nbsp;&nbsp; would have no space at all for anyone to exist.&nbsp; A version with only three trillion ants is going&nbsp;&nbsp; to cause serious ecological disasters as the food&nbsp; chain collapses. Good game tuning has a lot more&nbsp;&nbsp; in common with musical composition than it does&nbsp; hard science. It requires harmonious choices,&nbsp;&nbsp; purposeful and intentful imbalance of volume&nbsp; and frequency and tempo to achieve the desired&nbsp;&nbsp; emotional effect. What works in one song won't&nbsp; necessarily work in another, which means one&nbsp;&nbsp; game's right answers might be totally wrong&nbsp; for another. All aspects of your game need&nbsp;&nbsp; to harmonize and come together to be stronger&nbsp; than the sum of all of its parts. I call this&nbsp;&nbsp; tuning for harmony. When tuning a game, you're the&nbsp; conductor. Your job is to lead players emotionally&nbsp;&nbsp; where you'd like them to go, not follow the&nbsp; players whims or manipulate telemetry numbers.&nbsp;&nbsp; A game that is tuned for harmony is trying to&nbsp; achieve retention by creating a game state in&nbsp;&nbsp; which the highest number of players can each have&nbsp; their own unique brand of fun, express themselves,&nbsp;&nbsp; and stay engaged. This is a harmonious environment&nbsp; where joy and passion can thrive. Any imbalance&nbsp;&nbsp; that you put into place with intent is based on&nbsp; your vision for the game there to make it more&nbsp;&nbsp; interesting and exciting. It isn't an accident.&nbsp; Mathematical imbalance in your telemetry is not&nbsp;&nbsp; seen as a problem under this lens. It could be a&nbsp; symptom of a problem sometimes, but it could just&nbsp;&nbsp; as well be that the imbalance actually makes the&nbsp; hole stronger. How will you know the difference?&nbsp;&nbsp; Well, in order to tune for harmony, you're going&nbsp; to need a few things. First, you're going to need&nbsp;&nbsp; to put someone on your team in charge of game&nbsp; tuning. And that person needs to be able to play&nbsp;&nbsp; at a high enough level to feel the real game.&nbsp; They don't have to be tournament champions or&nbsp;&nbsp; the best in the world, but they should be strong&nbsp; enough to play alongside players of that caliber.&nbsp;&nbsp; This player needs to be under a few mandates.&nbsp; Number one, they can't play in tournaments. So,&nbsp;&nbsp; they can't be selfish about tuning. Not saying no&nbsp; one on your team can compete. I'm just suggesting&nbsp;&nbsp; that this one person should not compete in the&nbsp; game that you are making. They can feel free to&nbsp;&nbsp; compete in other games to scratch that itch.&nbsp; Number two, they shouldn't even have a main&nbsp;&nbsp; character or weapon. They should spend their play&nbsp; time using the characters or weapons the community&nbsp;&nbsp; think are the weakest and against strong players&nbsp; using the characters or weapons people think are&nbsp;&nbsp; the most offending to see if they even agree.&nbsp; Number three, they should try to think of the game&nbsp;&nbsp; as a whole. Play the whole roster relatively well&nbsp; and understand what aspects of each character are&nbsp;&nbsp; the most core to their identity and fun factor. A&nbsp; player who, say, only uses grapplers or only uses&nbsp;&nbsp; shotguns and can't get out of their comfort zone&nbsp; is going to struggle in this role. Number four,&nbsp;&nbsp; they should try to understand the feelings&nbsp; of players at various skill levels and keep&nbsp;&nbsp; each bracket of players in mind when tuning. You&nbsp; don't tune to give weaker players a chance against&nbsp;&nbsp; more experienced players, but you do need to tune&nbsp; against inexperienced players unique frustrations&nbsp;&nbsp; if you want to retain them. This can be a&nbsp; challenging set of asks for a member of your team,&nbsp;&nbsp; but I believe it's crucial. This person is&nbsp; your lantern in a dark cave. Without them,&nbsp;&nbsp; you'll be lost and you'll spend most of your time&nbsp; guessing your way back to the light. If you don't&nbsp;&nbsp; have this person on your team, you're going to&nbsp; have to find them externally and hire them. Next,&nbsp;&nbsp; listen to your players. Seriously, players lie,&nbsp; but you still need to hear them. Players are often&nbsp;&nbsp; right about the symptoms, even if they don't&nbsp; understand the best ways to fix the problems.&nbsp;&nbsp; If you can find a few players who love your game&nbsp; and have a better big picture sense than most, and&nbsp;&nbsp; talk to them a lot. These players are your canary&nbsp; in the coal mine. Don't take what they say at face&nbsp;&nbsp; value. Always think critically, but a discussion&nbsp; with these key people can lead you to the right&nbsp;&nbsp; choices much more quickly and accurately or keep&nbsp; you from making major mistakes. on KI. Of the&nbsp;&nbsp; hundreds of players I spoke to, I trusted exactly&nbsp; two to give me the kind of feedback that helped&nbsp;&nbsp; me validate or make tuning decisions and maybe&nbsp; 10 more to give me thoughts that were helpful. I&nbsp;&nbsp; learned who was who by chatting with the players&nbsp; a lot and being observant. Even with their help,&nbsp;&nbsp; we didn't make the right choice 100% of the time.&nbsp; And you won't either, but you should try to find&nbsp;&nbsp; your key players and make your success rate&nbsp; stronger. As you get information from telemetry&nbsp;&nbsp; and player sentiment reports, filter it and test&nbsp; against it rigorously. It's critical that you do&nbsp;&nbsp; not knee-jerk react to the things you hear. And it&nbsp; can be extremely difficult not to when influencer&nbsp;&nbsp; group think pressure campaigns arrive at your&nbsp; doorstep. You need to deploy changes quickly&nbsp;&nbsp; enough to minimize frustration. But you need&nbsp; to be measured enough to know when a problem&nbsp;&nbsp; is being overblown or a solution that works for&nbsp; your game has not yet been found. As an example,&nbsp;&nbsp; in Killer Instinct and Rumbleverse, I found that&nbsp; an average of 3 to four weeks work for non-c&nbsp;&nbsp; catastrophic issues based on those games audiences&nbsp; and goals. For catastrophic issues, every day&nbsp;&nbsp; counts, and you need to get those fixes out in 2&nbsp; to 3 days, if possible, while communicating often&nbsp;&nbsp; with the community. In most phases of gamedev,&nbsp; there's a mountain of work to do and not enough&nbsp;&nbsp; time to do it all. So, how do you prioritize your&nbsp; work and attention? During development, before&nbsp;&nbsp; you even have players, you need to spend time and&nbsp; energy on features that will let you deploy quick&nbsp;&nbsp; game-tuning changes without full and expensive&nbsp; title updates. These hot fix systems could&nbsp;&nbsp; literally save your game's life. Once your game&nbsp; is out, stay alert for mega frustrators, things&nbsp;&nbsp; in the game that are so far out of bounds that&nbsp; players won't tolerate them until your next major&nbsp;&nbsp; patch. Use your hot fix system and nuke these from&nbsp; orbit. There's a lot of competition for players&nbsp;&nbsp; attention, so don't give them an excuse to quit&nbsp; and play something else. Early on in Rumbleverse,&nbsp;&nbsp; players discovered a bug when double bouncing&nbsp; using a stop sign weapon that allowed them to&nbsp;&nbsp; safely drop a city block sized instant kill damage&nbsp; zone with zero counterplay. Our next patch was 5&nbsp;&nbsp; weeks away, and our user base would have shrunk to&nbsp; near nothing in mere days if we'd had been unable&nbsp;&nbsp; to fix this issue. Thanks to our hot fix system,&nbsp; we were able to get a fix deployed to players in&nbsp;&nbsp; a few days instead of the five weeks it would have&nbsp; taken if we had to wait for our next major patch,&nbsp;&nbsp; ensuring that most of the frustrated players&nbsp; retained. Nailing this built trust between us&nbsp;&nbsp; and the players so that if something like that&nbsp; ever happened again, they'd help calm each other&nbsp;&nbsp; down knowing that we'd likely fix it quickly.&nbsp; There are, of course, some common mistakes to&nbsp;&nbsp; avoid when tuning. You should avoid focusing on&nbsp; individual character versus character or team comp&nbsp;&nbsp; versus team comp matchup tuning. Conceptually,&nbsp; these things are big buckets of variables, and&nbsp;&nbsp; it's way too easy to get lost and cause unexpected&nbsp; knockdown effects in other areas of your game if&nbsp;&nbsp; you take on something so broad. You should instead&nbsp; spend time on much smaller and clearer details,&nbsp;&nbsp; which I'll discuss in this section. You also need&nbsp; to avoid overreacting or reacting too quickly if&nbsp;&nbsp; the severity of the issue isn't high. Judge&nbsp; severity by the level of frustration it seems&nbsp;&nbsp; to be causing. Validate it yourself by playing&nbsp; against it and see how pissed off you get.&nbsp;&nbsp; So after all that, what exactly is my method?&nbsp; First, I start by thinking about the big picture&nbsp;&nbsp; of risk versus reward across the entire game. So&nbsp; many tuning decisions can be more smartly made&nbsp;&nbsp; if you're able to correctly assess both the risk&nbsp; and reward of common actions in the game. Any new&nbsp;&nbsp; character or move you put in the game has to match&nbsp; this framework that you've conceptualized. Let's&nbsp;&nbsp; see some basic examples of risk versus reward and&nbsp; assess them. Think about head shot and shooters.&nbsp;&nbsp; If you aim for the body and you miss left&nbsp; or right, you hit the arms. If you miss low,&nbsp;&nbsp; you hit the legs. If you miss high, you might get&nbsp; a head shot. Your risk of missing when aiming for&nbsp;&nbsp; the body is at its lowest. And the reward is&nbsp; usually standard damage. If you aim for the&nbsp;&nbsp; head and you miss low, you hit the body and you&nbsp; get standard damage. But if you miss left, right,&nbsp;&nbsp; or high, you don't hit the target at all and&nbsp; deal no damage. Reward for a headshot is vastly&nbsp;&nbsp; increased damage output if you can land it. As a&nbsp; system, the riskreward of headshots makes logical&nbsp;&nbsp; and practical sense. This is a good example of an&nbsp; extremely common and effective riskreward system&nbsp;&nbsp; that breeds thoughtful play. As both aiming&nbsp; for the body or head are effective, but carry&nbsp;&nbsp; different levels of risk and reward that change as&nbsp; you switch weapons, distances, fight targets that&nbsp;&nbsp; move at different speeds, or even increase your&nbsp; own skill level. Now, let's look at a riskreward&nbsp;&nbsp; problem. Take for example Ultimate Marvel vs.&nbsp; Capcom 3. If you use Magneto's heavy attack,&nbsp;&nbsp; which is slower and harder to land to start your&nbsp; combo, your combo damage will be high enough to&nbsp;&nbsp; kill even the sturdiest characters in the game.&nbsp; However, if you start your combo with a quick&nbsp;&nbsp; light attack that comes out fast and hits low, and&nbsp; it's one of the easiest moves in the game to land,&nbsp;&nbsp; your combo damage will still be high enough to&nbsp; kill even the sturdiest characters in the game.&nbsp;&nbsp; The lower and higher risk options both have the&nbsp; same reward. So, in this case, skilled players&nbsp;&nbsp; will almost unanimously gravitate towards using&nbsp; low-risk attacks since the outcome is the same&nbsp;&nbsp; no matter what. Let's compare that to another&nbsp; game's take on this. In Guilty Gear Strive,&nbsp;&nbsp; using a quick punch or kick attack has less combo&nbsp; options and scales the combo's damage and hit stun&nbsp;&nbsp; duration more harshly. Using a slower slash or&nbsp; heavy slash attack gives you the highest damage&nbsp;&nbsp; combo starters and lets you combo more generously.&nbsp; The lower risk option here has a lower reward.&nbsp;&nbsp; This gives players a reason to use more of their&nbsp; options in various situations rather than falling&nbsp;&nbsp; back to the easy and quick ones. The next thing&nbsp; to look out for when hunting riskreward problems&nbsp;&nbsp; is unjustified inconsistency. Let's check out&nbsp; Killer Instinct. In KI, every character has a&nbsp;&nbsp; five-frame quick attack, but not every character&nbsp; has the same range or properties on their quickest&nbsp;&nbsp; attack. Not all of them get the same level of&nbsp; reward. Is this a problem? If the designers made&nbsp;&nbsp; these choices randomly, it might very well be.&nbsp; But if you deliberately design weaknesses into&nbsp;&nbsp; the character kits to compensate for their more&nbsp; extreme strengths, which is usually where their&nbsp;&nbsp; identity and fun lie, it could be perfectly okay&nbsp; to have a character whose quickest attack has poor&nbsp;&nbsp; range or one that can't be rapid fire canceled&nbsp; or one that can only successfully combo into one&nbsp;&nbsp; specific unsafe opener special move. Context&nbsp; is everything. Equality will flatline the&nbsp;&nbsp; play styles. Riskreward should make sense within&nbsp; each character, but also across all characters.&nbsp;&nbsp; Consider the characters Saberwolf, who is one&nbsp; of the easiest characters to play as, and Arya,&nbsp;&nbsp; who is the most difficult character in the game&nbsp; to play as. As I mentioned before, high difficulty&nbsp;&nbsp; is a risk, as the player has way more mistakes&nbsp; they could conceivably make in a match, and their&nbsp;&nbsp; options may be much more difficult to optimize.&nbsp; In a game tuned for flatness, perhaps Saberwolf&nbsp;&nbsp; and Arya should have a similar potential at top&nbsp; levels of play. But when balancing for harmony,&nbsp;&nbsp; we must acknowledge that Arya's high difficulty&nbsp; means she should have a higher number of top level&nbsp;&nbsp; advantages than other characters. Her higher risk&nbsp; should be justified by a higher potential reward.&nbsp;&nbsp; If an easier character could match her potential,&nbsp; almost no one would invest time into the&nbsp;&nbsp; character. Imbalance can absolutely ruin a game.&nbsp; Or imbalance could create harmony. How? If each&nbsp;&nbsp; character's moves are not built equally, there's&nbsp; an imbalance in their strengths and weaknesses.&nbsp;&nbsp; Without the imbalance of high-risk, high-reward&nbsp; characters living alongside low-risk, low-reward&nbsp;&nbsp; characters, player identity gets stifled. You need&nbsp; to find the right mix. So long as the riskreward&nbsp;&nbsp; values across your game make sense together,&nbsp; player identities will shine through and create&nbsp;&nbsp; variety and reduce repetitive play patterns. For&nbsp; instance, low or no risk tactics that have high&nbsp;&nbsp; rewards, such as safe jumps in fighting games,&nbsp; can be simultaneously boring for the attacker&nbsp;&nbsp; and very frustrating for the defender. Try to use&nbsp; this line of thinking to identify outliers and&nbsp;&nbsp; then study the characters or situations these&nbsp; outliers belong to so you can understand if&nbsp;&nbsp; they're a problem or not. Be purposeful with&nbsp; your design. Build in deliberate strengths&nbsp;&nbsp; and weaknesses and commit to them. This is not&nbsp; scientific. The developer responsible for game&nbsp;&nbsp; tuning is going to need a strong vision, a clear&nbsp; understanding of their target audience, and the&nbsp;&nbsp; ability to step back and try to feel all of this&nbsp; from a distance and see the big picture. The next&nbsp;&nbsp; thing you need to stay on top of is frustration.&nbsp; The opposite of frustration is fun. And so,&nbsp;&nbsp; these exist on a single scale together. Some&nbsp; frustration is okay, and it can even be good for&nbsp;&nbsp; your game so long as frustration doesn't overtake&nbsp; fun for your target audience. Imagine leaping off&nbsp;&nbsp; a building in a game with fall damage versus one&nbsp; without. A game without fall damage is definitely&nbsp;&nbsp; less frustrating, but it also lacks the adrenaline&nbsp; rush of attempting the leap and finding a way to&nbsp;&nbsp; land safely despite the danger. Neither of these&nbsp; approaches are wrong. It's just that each better&nbsp;&nbsp; suits a different audience. When an individual's&nbsp; frustration outweighs their fun, they quit. In&nbsp;&nbsp; a single player game, this part's really easy. In&nbsp; Zelda Breath of the Wild, the fun is in exploring&nbsp;&nbsp; and traversing this massive handcrafted world,&nbsp; solving puzzles, getting into battles, and then&nbsp;&nbsp; you have to interact with the very frustrating&nbsp; menus to cook food and manage your inventory,&nbsp;&nbsp; and then all of your weapons break. Some parts of&nbsp; the game are fun, and some parts are frustrating.&nbsp;&nbsp; They pull on each other within me to help me&nbsp; decide if I should keep playing or quit. So,&nbsp;&nbsp; let's explain the fun frustration scale a bit&nbsp; better. It weighs my own personal fun versus my&nbsp;&nbsp; own personal frustration. This scale represents&nbsp; me, not the game itself. This scale is not about&nbsp;&nbsp; truth. It's about my relationship with the game.&nbsp; If the fun side weighs more, I keep playing. I'll&nbsp;&nbsp; place weights that represent my personal enjoyment&nbsp; from exploration, puzzles, and combat on the left&nbsp;&nbsp; side. The fun side of the scale is heavier now,&nbsp; and so it moves down. Fun weighs more. And now&nbsp;&nbsp; I'll place weights that represent my own personal&nbsp; frustration from having to cook or navigate menus&nbsp;&nbsp; or when my weapons break. Maybe the weight of your&nbsp; personal frustration from say weapons breaking is&nbsp;&nbsp; less than mine. And that would be reflected on&nbsp; your own personal version of the scale. As you&nbsp;&nbsp; can see, the total weight of my fun in Breath of&nbsp; the Wild is heavier than the total weight of my&nbsp;&nbsp; frustrations. If we make the cooking interface a&nbsp; little better, the weight of my total frustration&nbsp;&nbsp; lowers, but the weight of my fun doesn't increase&nbsp; because improving the cooking interface doesn't&nbsp;&nbsp; improve the exploration, even though it does&nbsp; improve my overall relationship with the game.&nbsp;&nbsp; Remember, the lower side of the scale is the one&nbsp; that's winning out. Even in competitive games,&nbsp;&nbsp; some frustration is totally unrelated to gameplay&nbsp; aspects of the product. Like if it takes you 3&nbsp;&nbsp; minutes to simply log into the game and another 8&nbsp; minutes to find a match. But on the gameplay side&nbsp;&nbsp; of competitive games, this concept is a series&nbsp; of landmines because it is extremely common that&nbsp;&nbsp; one player's fun is exactly the other player's&nbsp; frustration. The more fun you let a player have,&nbsp;&nbsp; the more frustrated their opponent on the&nbsp; receiving end of that fun is likely to be. I&nbsp;&nbsp; think we all understand that players quit because&nbsp; frustration overtakes fun. And this obviously&nbsp;&nbsp; happens when the weight of the frustration side&nbsp; of the scale gets heavier. But it can also happen&nbsp;&nbsp; if the weight of the fun side gets lighter. If I&nbsp; make something less frustrating for the victim,&nbsp;&nbsp; it may reduce fun for the attacker. It's very&nbsp; often zero sum. In this example, this individual's&nbsp;&nbsp; frustration about being hit wasn't very high in&nbsp; the first place and didn't change when combos&nbsp;&nbsp; got shorter. But because they enjoyed doing long&nbsp; combos so much, the weight of their fun dropped,&nbsp;&nbsp; suddenly causing frustration to outweigh the fun&nbsp; for them. This change may have drastically reduced&nbsp;&nbsp; the frustration for another player and improved&nbsp; their personal scale while causing this particular&nbsp;&nbsp; player to consider quitting. In the gameplay&nbsp; of competitive games, you generally can't make&nbsp;&nbsp; things universally better for everyone. There will&nbsp; almost always be a give and take. Because of this,&nbsp;&nbsp; you need to communicate heavily with and keep an&nbsp; eye on your community to see frustration trends&nbsp;&nbsp; appearing, and you need to move quickly to test&nbsp; against them to see how valid you believe they&nbsp;&nbsp; are. Some frustrations can be healthy for a game.&nbsp; Remember, this is an ecosystem. High highs are&nbsp;&nbsp; rarely possible without low lows. What you need&nbsp; to look out for are mega frustrators, things that&nbsp;&nbsp; are so annoying to deal with that no matter how&nbsp; fair their riskreward values may seem that they&nbsp;&nbsp; have to be tuned or you're going to rapidly lose&nbsp; chunks of your audience. We often only make game&nbsp;&nbsp; tuning decisions around risk and reward with top&nbsp; level play in mind. We do this because factually&nbsp;&nbsp; mid and lower level players are not able to&nbsp; observe the whole of the known game yet and are&nbsp;&nbsp; extremely unlikely to notice the riskreward tuning&nbsp; that we do. But when tuning against frustration,&nbsp;&nbsp; we need to consider all levels of play. In Killer&nbsp; Instinct, Gargos has a portal punch move, a&nbsp;&nbsp; tracking projectile that can start a ranged combo.&nbsp; This move was easier to deal with at higher levels&nbsp;&nbsp; of play. Its riskreward values mostly made sense.&nbsp; It had counterplay, and it fit the character's kit&nbsp;&nbsp; really well. But at mid to low levels of&nbsp; play, this move became a mega frustrator.&nbsp;&nbsp; The answers to it, while available and plentiful,&nbsp; were not apparent enough at those levels of play,&nbsp;&nbsp; and the move was causing a number of players to&nbsp; threaten to quit. We tested against this claim&nbsp;&nbsp; as best as we could and ultimately agreed that&nbsp; this move had crossed the line for that level&nbsp;&nbsp; of play. As a result, we adjusted the move quite&nbsp; a few times to find a spot that still worked for&nbsp;&nbsp; top level play, but was much less frustrating at&nbsp; other levels of play. Even at low levels of play,&nbsp;&nbsp; if a player feels like their opponent can&nbsp; beat them with just one brain deadad tactic,&nbsp;&nbsp; which they'll often call spam, they'll frustrate&nbsp; out of the game. Importantly, there is a limit to&nbsp;&nbsp; how weak we were willing to make this move. After&nbsp; a certain point, we had to let the community know&nbsp;&nbsp; that we were not taking the move out of the game&nbsp; and that if they were struggling to deal with&nbsp;&nbsp; this version of the move, they'd need to practice.&nbsp; Our goal isn't to solve the problem for everyone,&nbsp;&nbsp; but to reach a compromise that still might ask&nbsp; some players to overcome their frustrations.&nbsp;&nbsp; If you show your community that you're listening&nbsp; and they believe in you, they will invest effort&nbsp;&nbsp; on their side more readily to overcome challenges&nbsp; and minor frustrations. Meeting you in the middle,&nbsp;&nbsp; that means sometimes, yes, asking players to learn&nbsp; or practice is a part of the bargain. Speaking&nbsp;&nbsp; of brain dead stuff, we need to prevent people&nbsp; from getting bored. On a momentto- moment level,&nbsp;&nbsp; this makes thoughtless gameplay our enemy. You're&nbsp; spending a lot of time not making meaningful&nbsp;&nbsp; decisions. Even if the base actions feel great and&nbsp; have great feedback, you'll eventually get bored.&nbsp;&nbsp; Engagement is the result of making a decision and&nbsp; then seeing the rewarding or punishing results&nbsp;&nbsp; of that decision. Remember our rumbleverse stop&nbsp; sign nuke example? This technique was extremely&nbsp;&nbsp; frustrating to get hit by, but was super fun&nbsp; and funny to do to people at first. But once&nbsp;&nbsp; you mastered the movement needed to do it, which&nbsp; to be honest wasn't very hard at all, it became a&nbsp;&nbsp; thoughtless way to play. You'd land in the world,&nbsp; find a stop sign, nuke a city block, repeat,&nbsp;&nbsp; brain off. So even the people using and abusing&nbsp; the technique or experiencing disengagement due to&nbsp;&nbsp; the degenerate play pattern the stop sign nuke&nbsp; represented. Long combos or block strings in&nbsp;&nbsp; fighting games with zero or infrequent defensive&nbsp; mechanics can also cause a lot of disengagement.&nbsp;&nbsp; Players across many genres do not respond well&nbsp; to losing control of their character. In fighting&nbsp;&nbsp; games, you lose control of your character every&nbsp; time you get hit. My own smallcale studies show&nbsp;&nbsp; players starting to disengage and have frustration&nbsp; spikes on average between the 6 and 8second marks&nbsp;&nbsp; of losing control of their character. Obviously,&nbsp; some individuals, especially in the FGC, have an&nbsp;&nbsp; extreme tolerance to this and can routinely sit&nbsp; through repetitive 40-cond long combos on the&nbsp;&nbsp; receiving end, but this in my experience is not a&nbsp; critical mass of people. I'm not saying you should&nbsp;&nbsp; never make a game with long combos. I'm just&nbsp; suggesting that you need to understand the kind&nbsp;&nbsp; of audience you're trying to retain. And if the&nbsp; long combos do exist, find ways to make them more&nbsp;&nbsp; varied and/or less frequent. Disengaged players&nbsp; on defense are very likely to quit. But disengaged&nbsp;&nbsp; players on offense are, believe it or not, also&nbsp; likely to quit. Game balance and target audience&nbsp;&nbsp; are extremely related. It's not just that the&nbsp; audience has its own feelings about game balance&nbsp;&nbsp; and what frustrations weigh the most to them, but&nbsp; also that different types of game balance attract&nbsp;&nbsp; and repel different types of audiences. and&nbsp; different audiences self- select into different&nbsp;&nbsp; types of games and game balance outcomes. Let's&nbsp; look at three example scales. In the first,&nbsp;&nbsp; developers worked very hard to sand off every&nbsp; frustration they could, regardless of how much fun&nbsp;&nbsp; had to go to achieve that. Even though the weight&nbsp; of the frustration side is light, so is the weight&nbsp;&nbsp; of the fun side of the scale. This can result in&nbsp; even very minor frustrations feeling oversized and&nbsp;&nbsp; make spending time with the game feel not worth it&nbsp; because the fun it delivers is sterile or bland.&nbsp;&nbsp; Players of this game have less reasons to quit,&nbsp; yes, but they also have less reasons to play. In&nbsp;&nbsp; the second scale, developers didn't really care&nbsp; about frustrators. So, this theoretical game has&nbsp;&nbsp; a very high frustration weight, but it also has a&nbsp; very high fun weight. You'll notice that the ratio&nbsp;&nbsp; of the scale is similar to the first, but the&nbsp; actual weight of each side matters a great deal.&nbsp;&nbsp; While the audience may be smaller in this type of&nbsp; game, the immense weight of the fun side of the&nbsp;&nbsp; scale is going to have the players who can deal&nbsp; with the high level of frustration calling this&nbsp;&nbsp; a favorite game. Some players call these kinds of&nbsp; games kusog, Japanese slang for shitty game. They&nbsp;&nbsp; say it lovingly and disparagingly all at once.&nbsp; It's fascinating. In the final scale, which is&nbsp;&nbsp; probably the ideal goal for developers for most&nbsp; projects, frustrations were addressed carefully in&nbsp;&nbsp; ways that while inevitably did lower the weight of&nbsp; the fun side a bit, didn't overdo it. This scale&nbsp;&nbsp; is indeed the healthiest of the three examples, as&nbsp; the weight of the fun is still high and it vastly&nbsp;&nbsp; outweighs the frustration side. That's why it's&nbsp; so important to know your audience. None of these&nbsp;&nbsp; three results are wrong or bad. They just serve&nbsp; different people. As you tune your competitive&nbsp;&nbsp; game, you need to keep your target audience in&nbsp; mind. I highly suggest using Quantic Foundaries&nbsp;&nbsp; data on player motivation to help segment&nbsp; your audience into buckets you can more easily&nbsp;&nbsp; understand. There will be people outside of your&nbsp; target audience who will try your game, and the&nbsp;&nbsp; majority of these people are unretainable. In this&nbsp; example, our core audience member on the left is&nbsp;&nbsp; happy, but our player from outside the core group&nbsp; on the right is having less fun because this isn't&nbsp;&nbsp; their usual kind of game, and their unfamiliarity&nbsp; adds even more frustration. If the weight of their&nbsp;&nbsp; frustration is so high that reducing some of it&nbsp; still leaves their frustration outweighing their&nbsp;&nbsp; fun, the game just isn't for them. But if you&nbsp; insist on trying to reduce the weight of their&nbsp;&nbsp; frustration, you may be cutting away at the fun&nbsp; of your core audience, which could also result&nbsp;&nbsp; in some of their frustration suddenly outweighing&nbsp; their fun. In this example, we made changes that&nbsp;&nbsp; made the game less frustrating for people outside&nbsp; the core audience by changing things in the game&nbsp;&nbsp; that were not frustrating at all to the core&nbsp; users. The result of that was a loss of fun&nbsp;&nbsp; for the core players. We failed to make enough of&nbsp; a dent to retain people outside the core group,&nbsp;&nbsp; and now we've put a portion of our core audience&nbsp; at risk of quitting, too. Not every edge needs&nbsp;&nbsp; softening. If you're lucky enough to make a game&nbsp; that lasts for quite a long time, you may also&nbsp;&nbsp; encounter players who, despite loving your game&nbsp; and thinking that it's relatively well tuned,&nbsp;&nbsp; are becoming bored from repetition. At this time,&nbsp; you'll have to weigh the reward of doing some kind&nbsp;&nbsp; of tuning shakeup to get people re-engaged.&nbsp; against the risk of that action frustrating&nbsp;&nbsp; a vocal and influential part of your community.&nbsp; The Street Fighter 6 community is going through&nbsp;&nbsp; this right now as of filming in early 2026. Many&nbsp; in the community feel the game is well tuned,&nbsp;&nbsp; but still want a big shakeup anyway because&nbsp; they are becoming bored. Matches are lacking in&nbsp;&nbsp; surprise or discovery, and the feeling of I've&nbsp; seen it all is hurting their experience. And&nbsp;&nbsp; finally, we get back to play pattern optimization.&nbsp; Optimization is the enemy. I'm not talking about&nbsp;&nbsp; software performance here. I'm talking about&nbsp; players optimizing their gameplay choices to&nbsp;&nbsp; minimize risk and maximize reward. Optimal combos,&nbsp; option selects, unreachable map positioning,&nbsp;&nbsp; etc. You need to make a game where the right&nbsp; answers are much more obscured, or better yet,&nbsp;&nbsp; much more plentiful. You want a game where&nbsp; surprise and discovery can continue for as&nbsp;&nbsp; long as possible post launch. For instance,&nbsp; Ultimate Marvel vs. Capcom 3's fast-paced,&nbsp;&nbsp; neutral, and rapid decision-making is one of the&nbsp; best parts of the game, and has lots of surprises&nbsp;&nbsp; and memorable moments, even 15 years later. But&nbsp; when I land a hit with virtually any attack,&nbsp;&nbsp; it becomes very clear what I should do. I should&nbsp; perform my very long combo with little to no&nbsp;&nbsp; reason for variation and kill your character. This&nbsp; optimal play gives me maximum reward with minimum&nbsp;&nbsp; decision-making, so long as I can execute, and&nbsp; takes up a large portion of the time spent playing&nbsp;&nbsp; during any match. During the combo, a skilled&nbsp; attacker is only engaged at the start as they&nbsp;&nbsp; try to stabilize the opponent and decide if they&nbsp; need to burn Xactor or any meter. The defender&nbsp;&nbsp; should try to engage the entire time, no matter&nbsp; how long the combo, in case the combo drops on&nbsp;&nbsp; accident or a reset is attempted. But focusing for&nbsp; that long without meaningful decisions to make is&nbsp;&nbsp; exhausting, and it also results in disengagement&nbsp; and frustration. Street Fighter 6 steps it up&nbsp;&nbsp; by obscuring optimal combos quite a bit better&nbsp; than Marvel vs. Capcom 3. When you score a hit,&nbsp;&nbsp; the starter you used can matter a lot more. You&nbsp; need to look at screen position, your drive meter,&nbsp;&nbsp; your opponent's drive meter, your health,&nbsp; your opponent's health, what round it is,&nbsp;&nbsp; your own super meter conditions to make sure you&nbsp; can decide how to best optimize what combo to do,&nbsp;&nbsp; how much resources to spend. This game is much&nbsp; harder to optimize, but ultimately it can be&nbsp;&nbsp; done. Top level play in Street Fighter 6 after a&nbsp; while has virtually every player using the same&nbsp;&nbsp; combos in similar situations once those players&nbsp; are fluent enough in the game to know the optimal&nbsp;&nbsp; answer in each situation. Though you do see some&nbsp; player expression variation with some high-risk&nbsp;&nbsp; players spending more drive meter to burn&nbsp; themselves out on purpose more frequently, while&nbsp;&nbsp; others are more conservative with their gauge&nbsp; if the combo isn't going to kill or checkmate.&nbsp;&nbsp; Street Fighter 6 makes the right answers more&nbsp; plentiful, more diverse in riskreward values,&nbsp;&nbsp; and they take longer for players to optimize&nbsp; because there are so many variables. Ideally,&nbsp;&nbsp; you want to make a game where instead of the right&nbsp; answers being difficult but ultimately possible to&nbsp;&nbsp; optimize, players are presented with a variety&nbsp; of correct answers, each representing their&nbsp;&nbsp; own riskreward values. So, instead of a community&nbsp; working together to solve the game like a puzzle,&nbsp;&nbsp; after which conformity of play style begins to&nbsp; occur, players will instead focus on making the&nbsp;&nbsp; choices that best fit their own personalities.&nbsp; Player expression breeds variety. Imagine a series&nbsp;&nbsp; of possible combos all starting from the same hit&nbsp; confirm. Each does more damage than the last, but&nbsp;&nbsp; is also harder to execute than the last. This may&nbsp; seem like a proper setup for risk and reward. And&nbsp;&nbsp; it isn't a bad way to start, but at top levels of&nbsp; play where execution starts to become irrelevant,&nbsp;&nbsp; what you'll get is a push towards optimization&nbsp; and conformity instead of expression and variety.&nbsp;&nbsp; Trying to create a system in which different&nbsp; combo routes give expressly different outcomes&nbsp;&nbsp; and have their own advantages and disadvantages&nbsp; beyond executional requirements will ensure that&nbsp;&nbsp; players can play their own way. Variety isn't&nbsp; just in character or weapon selection. It's also&nbsp;&nbsp; found within the play styles of the people who&nbsp; use the same characters or weapons if your game&nbsp;&nbsp; is harmonizing correctly. Harmony is not about&nbsp; making it hard for players to find the right&nbsp;&nbsp; answer. It's about giving them many right answers&nbsp; and letting each player lean towards their own&nbsp;&nbsp; favorites. In game design, all things should&nbsp; be done with intent. If someone asks me why I&nbsp;&nbsp; made a recent design decision and my answer is,&nbsp; I don't know, then I messed up. I may be forced&nbsp;&nbsp; to make a suboptimal decision from time to time&nbsp; due to various circumstances beyond my control,&nbsp;&nbsp; but I should still be able to clearly express why&nbsp; the decision was made. And you need to work very&nbsp;&nbsp; hard to make sure your players know that you&nbsp; move with intent. This means your patch notes&nbsp;&nbsp; need to communicate both what you're doing and&nbsp; why you're doing it. You need clear, detailed,&nbsp;&nbsp; thorough notes or videos that include reasons why&nbsp; your team chose these changes. Even if players&nbsp;&nbsp; disagree with your reasoning, they should be&nbsp; able to see clear intent. If they can see intent,&nbsp;&nbsp; trust will build and it will often keep them from&nbsp; labeling you as someone blindly throwing darts to&nbsp;&nbsp; choose balance adjustments. I originally wrote&nbsp; a version of this talk that you're watching now&nbsp;&nbsp; back in 2019. And in the time between then and&nbsp; now, I'm very happy to report that developers&nbsp;&nbsp; across all the games that I play and watch have&nbsp; improved drastically in the area of patch notes.&nbsp;&nbsp; Keep it up. Thank you. As you tune, you will&nbsp; make mistakes. However, a community that has&nbsp;&nbsp; trust and confidence in you will tolerate those&nbsp; mistakes with lower levels of frustration and will&nbsp;&nbsp; generally perceive the state of the game's balance&nbsp; more favorably. Because after all, game balance is&nbsp;&nbsp; mostly just vibes. vibes that you have a heavy&nbsp; hand in establishing and influencing. Remember,&nbsp;&nbsp; the process is not hear about the problem followed&nbsp; by fix the problem. Process needs to be hear about&nbsp;&nbsp; the problem. Investigate and decide if you even&nbsp; agree it's a real problem. Use everything you've&nbsp;&nbsp; learned to find a solution to the problem that&nbsp; weighs all of the other problems that need solving&nbsp;&nbsp; and how that solve might hurt or destabilize&nbsp; other parts of the game and the audience. And then&nbsp;&nbsp; communicate with your players. So, to wrap this&nbsp; up, I believe a balanced roster isn't one where&nbsp;&nbsp; every character has an equal shot at winning,&nbsp; but it's one where there's a little something for&nbsp;&nbsp; every type of player within your core audience.&nbsp; I once heard a player ask why developers couldn't&nbsp;&nbsp; just balance a game before it came out. And as&nbsp; I hope you understand by now, that would be an&nbsp;&nbsp; impossible task because the audience, who will&nbsp; eventually decide what balance even means to them,&nbsp;&nbsp; haven't even touched a game yet. Tuning for&nbsp; harmony is my personal method of game tuning.&nbsp;&nbsp; served me well across KI and Rumbleverse. And I&nbsp; hope you learned a lot about the goals and hazards&nbsp;&nbsp; of game tuning from this talk. If you're in charge&nbsp; of tuning a competitive game, you should do what&nbsp;&nbsp; works for you and your community. If you really&nbsp; believe in tuning for flatness or whatever method&nbsp;&nbsp; you use and it's working for your team and you're&nbsp; achieving your goals, that's rad. Keep doing that.&nbsp;&nbsp; If you want to try some or all of my methods,&nbsp; that's cool, too. I'll make myself available for&nbsp;&nbsp; consulting with folks in the industry who do this&nbsp; kind of work. If people want that, just hit me up&nbsp;&nbsp; on Blue Sky or wherever and we can work something&nbsp; out. Whatever your personal takeaways are,&nbsp;&nbsp; remember that game balance isn't real. It's not&nbsp; a hard objective thing that we can measure and&nbsp;&nbsp; take scientific actions to fix. In reality, it's&nbsp; just a person's fully subjective perception. And&nbsp;&nbsp; not only that, our views can change on it even&nbsp; by the day and even when the game itself hasn't&nbsp;&nbsp; been adjusted at all. Instead of fixating so&nbsp; strongly on something so impossible to pin down,&nbsp;&nbsp; I believe designers should focus on much&nbsp; more important things when tuning a game.&nbsp;&nbsp; Those things are communicating clearly with&nbsp; your audience, minimizing their frustrations&nbsp;&nbsp; quickly and thoughtfully, and keeping them engaged&nbsp; with lots of interesting decisions to make, and&nbsp;&nbsp; surprising them with cool new interactions each&nbsp; time they play. And most of all, as a dev tuning&nbsp;&nbsp; a game or a player reacting to patch notes, don't&nbsp; panic. If you made it to the end of the video,&nbsp;&nbsp; I hope this gets your brain flowing and makes&nbsp; discourse around game tuning a little stronger&nbsp;&nbsp; overall. And maybe as a bonus, uh, it encourages&nbsp; gamers to give the devs who do game tuning a&nbsp;&nbsp; little more grace. I have a lot more to say on&nbsp; this topic, so condensing it down into this still&nbsp;&nbsp; pretty long video is quite the challenge. If you&nbsp; have follow-up questions or want to chat sometime,&nbsp;&nbsp; just drop a comment and uh, I'll I'll try to&nbsp; check it out. I want to thank DoubleA for his&nbsp;&nbsp; hard work helping me write, execute, and edit this&nbsp; video that I've wanted to make for so long. I'd&nbsp;&nbsp; also like to thank Noah Sasso, Ultra David, and&nbsp; Filament, Mean Salty, and Ski Sonic for their help&nbsp;&nbsp; editing the script.   6. @MasterChef306 [1 likes]: There's so many fun anecdotes about how winrates don't tell the whole story, all across gaming.

In League, among other games in general, characters have been nerfed only to see their winrates *increase*, as players who'd only played them for perceived "overpowered" tools left to greener pastures while more dedicated and skilled players were left with their mains, still able to use them effectively.

In Overwatch, Ana was thought to be useless on release, and buffed repeatedly for *months*. Then, players discovered that if they played the whole game differently - organizing deathball strategies and even transitioning from 2 DPS, 2 Tank, 2 Support to 3 Tank, 3 Support team compositions - Ana was suddenly not only strong but downright overpowered. Eventually she had to be nerfed well below her power level on launch in order to prevent her from becoming a must-pick character in every game.

In Dota, some characters like Viper frequently have very high winrates, well in excess of 50% at top-tier play. However, that's not because the character is overpowered, but rather because Viper can hard-counter certain other characters due to some of his specific tools. Viper is a punish pick - he has a high winrate because even the act of choosing viper is performed as counterplay to an opponent's mistakes during the draft phase before players even load into the game.

Also in Dota is the Divine Rapier, an item with a 90% winrate. This is because the item is wildly overpowered - but on death, you drop the rapier, allowing the enemies to pick it up and use it against you. It wins 90% of games because the majority of the time, the team that wins the game has wiped the other team first, picking up the rapier if the wiped team had one.

  13. @zatharista: Man, the patchnotes subject... I really hope we can get to a good place with that someday. I know so many devs hate doing those because they take a long time to write or they feel people dont read them, but they're absolutely necessary.


Of course the opposite problem can always happen. Devs don't document things, take bad notes, dont include important changes in the notes, or just straight up lie about things. There are so many games where very important information is not communicated effectively anywhere in the game itself, so the only sources for said information is fan forums or wikis, which rely heavily on dev notes or resorting to datamining and hours and hours of experimentation.


Its a bad look either way, but try and be as thorough and descriptive with your notes as possible and clearly explain your intent with each change, as much as is reasonably possible. And most importantly PLEASE DON'T LIE. Sorting through all the changes is hard enough without having to confirm the validity of something, and it makes players lose trust in you!

If I want to be an Olympic skier, my trainer is going to have me go down that same slope that I'm very good at 4% faster or find a new slope that's 4% bumpier. They've studied this over and over again. 4% is just out of reach, but you know it's so close you'll get it in a practice or two, a session or two, a week or two. That'll become your new baseline. 2% is too easy. 6% is too overwhelming. So, one of the jobs is figure out your 4% of pushing yourself a little to be more, but in a safe way, and then add that as part of your practice, some sliver. And that's often called the 80/20 rule. That said, like SO many things, I don't think it's quite as black-and-white as we'd like to think. Those two paths are a spectrum, not a dichotomy. And while my initial experience with creating videos on other systems lined up with what you describe, I learned in the past year or so that it is completely possible to create videos about non-D&D systems as long as you're smart about the packaging. I'm actually seeing much more success with non-D&D videos now than I did in the wake of the OGL.

I've also found that while YouTube can definitely issue temporary punishments for straying off their preferred path, those punishments aren't a death sentence unless you fail to learn from them. I found that D&D advice videos were performing worse for me in the past year or so (plus, like you mentioned... I've already said most of what I want to say!) so I've been experimenting a lot more lately, and even though some of those experiments have definitely failed... some have succeeded! And no single flop has "killed" my channel. A lot of the creators who end up quitting over the algorithm are at the tail end of a long, downward slope. I'm not saying they HAVE to adapt – they should make what they want, and if what they want isn't performing anymore, that must be very painful. But they are making the choice to not adapt even while YouTube signals to them that their work is no longer resonating.

The tough pill to swallow is that being a YouTube creator, in any niche, is fucking hard. You have infinite competition, the environment you're creating in is constantly changing, and if you aren't constantly changing to keep up, you will fail. It is a highly demanding job that doesn't really reward legacy or labor – just results. I think of it as a temporary job the way that being, say, a professional athlete is a temporary job. Most people aren't going to be energized enough, resilient enough, tolerant enough, etc. to keep pace with the ups and downs of YouTube long-term. But personally, I'm unbelievably grateful that I get to make videos about fantasy games in my basement for a living, even if that's temporary. Every job has its benefits and its downsides, and for now, I'll choose the stressors of YouTube over the boredom and misery that traditional employment offered me.
